extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in the history of advertising and print culture (particularly medical quackery)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and characterize the features, persuasive techniques, and deceptive practices used in 17th–18th century medical and mountebank advertisements as described in a history-of-advertising text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to authority / royal or high-status appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of service to royalty or eminent persons (e.g., 'he has been Physician to 3 Emperours and 9 Kings', 'Queen Anne and George I. honoured Read with the care of their eyes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to convey legitimacy and impress the credulous; authors note how such claims misled the public and even secured knighthoods for impostors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Latin and learned-sounding fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Including 'a few scraps of Latin in his bills' to make the ignorant suppose the advertiser 'to be wonderfully learned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial learned language functions as a credibility signal even when substantive knowledge is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonials and affidavits from supposed patients
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements taking the form of recommendations or signed attestations (e.g., Richard Sandford's printed certificate about his son's cure; long case-notes describing recoveries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as independent proof of efficacy; often detailed with names, dates, and locations to strengthen plausibility but could be fabricated or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle-case anecdotes and detailed cure narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic stories of instantaneous or unlikely cures (e.g., woman in childbirth delivered 'in less than a Quarter of an Hour' after a small dose; poisoned dogs where one was saved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vivid anecdote is used to persuade readers; the text highlights such narratives as a common persuasive device of quacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of universal remedies / panaceas
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold assertions of one medicine curing 'all Diseases' or 'all Disorders in the Head' and similar universal claims ('cure all bodily but many mental evils').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked as an abuse and sign of imposture — an anti-pattern that signals quackery rather than genuine medical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public demonstrations and official-style tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to observed tests or trials (e.g., College of Physicians poisoning two dogs to test the horn powder; doctors asked to 'try if it would Expel Poyson').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers cited such demonstrations as quasi-official verification; the book records these to show how quacks exploited apparent empirical tests for credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seals, coats of arms, and authenticity markings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a printed seal or 'Coat of Arms' on remedies and warnings that products without the seal are 'Counterfeits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functioned as an authenticity marker to distinguish 'genuine' product from imitators; advertisers instructed purchasers to check for such signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear address/signage and instructions for locating the seller
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific location details and shop signs (e.g., 'Sign of the Moon and Stars', explicit street and court directions) included in bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing an exact address reduced purchaser confusion and reinforced apparent legitimacy—especially important for itinerant sellers who moved from place to place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price signaling and tiered pricing (appeal to different classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit price lists and differential pricing (e.g., 'sixpence', 'ten Guineas for a whole set', 'sold at this Price... in regard to the Poor only').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prices signaled value and accessibility; 'cheap' offers could attract the poor while high prices implied luxury/quality to the wealthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free advice as a hook (advice gratis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering 'Advice gratis' or 'The Poor may have Advice... for Nothing' as part of the advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to draw in customers; the text remarks on the irony that 'free' advice frequently led to purchases of remedies, and sometimes was effectively meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: No cure, no pay guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit warranties like 'No Cure no Pay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers used this promise as a trust device to reduce purchase risk and to compete with rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy and proprietary mystique
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of secret ingredients, exclusive virtues (e.g., 'I was not willing to part with [the Horn]'), and promises of 'profound Secrecy if required.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrecy created an aura of special knowledge and exclusivity; the narrative notes how this enhanced perceived value and trust among certain clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining unrelated professions/services
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverts mixing roles (e.g., 'Dentist and Dancing Master', 'Surgeon by Birth' plus dentist), or mountebank spectacles combined with medical sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conjunction could increase public appeal (entertainment plus remedy) but also indicated lack of specialization and prompted skepticism by professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spectacle, stagecraft, and itinerant performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountebanks and travelling shows with coaches, tumblers, rope-dancers, stages; selling 'packets for six-pence' alongside performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance attracted crowds and created demand; the book emphasizes how showmanship was an essential marketing tactic for itinerant quacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attacks on rivals as self-justifying publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings 'A Caution to the Unwary' and advertisements that denounce other pretenders to highlight the advertiser's superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used to position oneself as the honest alternative; the text points out the hypocrisy when attackers themselves puffed their own wares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of experience and enumerating cures/operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numeric claims about past successes (e.g., 'upwards of three thousand Operations and Cures') and dated lists of case outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers and case lists were used as empirical-seeming evidence; the author shows how such figures bolstered reputations even when unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed dosage and application instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise directions for use (e.g., 'The Powder must be put on a Linnen Cloath and applied to the Place, and take as much as will lie on a Six-pence for two Mornings in warm Ale').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific instructions lent an air of professional competence and allowed advertisers to appear authoritative and practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-status endorsements and noble clientele appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit claims that 'several of the Nobility' can attest or that cures were 'attested by several of the Nobility' and addressing adverts 'To the Nobility, Gentry & Others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorsements from high-status clients were leveraged to persuade broader audiences by social proof.
